---
title: "Trusting the Number: Probability Calibration in ML"
date: "2026-07-01"
categories: [machine learning, statistical inference]

## Background

Here is a confession: for years I treated the output of `predict_proba` as if it were an actual probability. The model said $0.9$, so I assumed that among all the cases it scored $0.9$, roughly $90\%$ were positive. For a logistic regression that reflex is mostly harmless. For a random forest, a boosted tree, or an SVM, it can be badly wrong — and the failure is silent, because the model's accuracy and AUC look perfectly fine while the numbers themselves lie.

That is what calibration is about: whether a predicted probability *means* what it says. A model can rank cases beautifully — every positive scored above every negative — and still be hopelessly miscalibrated, systematically over- or under-stating its confidence. Ranking and calibration are different virtues, and most of machine learning optimizes for the first while quietly assuming the second.

The reflex I want to bust is the opposite one, though: *always calibrate*. Calibration is not free, it is not always necessary, and applying it blindly can cost you. So I will walk through when the number actually needs to mean something, how to tell whether it does, and how to fix it when it doesn't.

## Notation

Consider binary classification with label $Y \in \{0, 1\}$ and a model that outputs a score $\hat{p}(X) \in [0, 1]$ meant to estimate $P(Y = 1 \mid X)$. The model is **perfectly calibrated** if

$$
P\big(Y = 1 \mid \hat{p}(X) = p\big) = p \quad \text{for all } p \in [0, 1].
$$

In words: of all the cases assigned score $p$, a fraction $p$ are truly positive. This is a property of the score's *marginal* relationship to the outcome, not of individual predictions — which is why a model can be calibrated and useless (predict the base rate for everyone) or sharp and miscalibrated (rank perfectly, wrong magnitudes). Good probabilities need both calibration *and* resolution (the tendency to push scores away from the base rate toward $0$ and $1$).

## A Closer Look

### When you actually need it

The single most useful question is: *does a downstream decision depend on the magnitude of the probability, or only on its order?*

If you only need to **rank** — show the top-$k$ most likely churners, sort leads by score, compute AUC — calibration is irrelevant. Any monotonic transform of the score leaves the ranking, and hence AUC, unchanged. Recalibrating buys you nothing here and, with isotonic regression, can even *hurt* by introducing ties.

Calibration starts to matter the moment a probability feeds arithmetic. Expected-value decisions ($\text{value} = p \cdot \text{gain} - (1-p) \cdot \text{cost}$) need the $p$ to be right, not just ordered. Thresholding at a fixed operating point (act when $p > 0.7$) assumes $0.7$ means something. Combining model outputs with other probabilities, feeding them to a Bayesian update, or reporting them to a human who will treat $0.9$ as "nearly certain" — all of these break under miscalibration. This is closely related to the distinction I drew between [causal and predictive models](https://vyasenov.github.io/blog/diff-causal-predictive-models.html): the use case dictates which properties of the output you are allowed to trust.

---

### Diagnosing miscalibration

The workhorse diagnostic is the **reliability diagram**: bin predictions by score, and for each bin plot the mean predicted probability (x-axis) against the observed fraction of positives (y-axis). Perfect calibration lies on the $45^\circ$ line. Curves below the diagonal signal over-confidence; curves above it, under-confidence. It is one of the plots I think everyone should have in their back pocket, alongside the [others worth knowing](https://vyasenov.github.io/blog/six-plots-you-should-know.html).

For a single number, use a *proper scoring rule* — one minimized in expectation by the true probabilities. The Brier score is the mean squared error of the probabilities,

$$
\text{Brier} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \big(\hat{p}_i - y_i\big)^2,
$$

and log loss is its logarithmic cousin. But mind the trap: by Murphy's decomposition, the Brier score splits into $\text{uncertainty} - \text{resolution} + \text{reliability}$. Only the reliability term is calibration. A model with better discrimination can post a lower Brier score *despite* being worse calibrated. So a proper scoring rule alone cannot tell you calibration is the problem — pair it with the reliability diagram, always.

---

### Which models, and why

Not all classifiers misbehave the same way. Logistic regression is typically well-calibrated out of the box: minimizing log loss with the canonical logit link enforces a balance property that ties predicted probabilities to observed frequencies. That is a real, if underappreciated, argument for the humble logit.

The common offenders fail in characteristic directions. Naive Bayes is *over-confident* — its independence assumption compounds evidence it should not, pushing scores toward $0$ and $1$. Random forests and bagged ensembles are *under-confident*: averaging many trees pulls probabilities toward the middle, since it is rare for all trees to agree at the extremes, producing a telltale sigmoid reliability curve. Max-margin methods like SVMs distort further still, because they optimize the decision boundary and never really estimate probabilities at all. Knowing the direction of a model's bias tells you which fix will suit it.

---

### Fixing it

Calibration is a post-processing step: fit a monotonic map from raw scores to calibrated probabilities on **held-out data**. The two classic choices trade flexibility against data hunger.

*Platt (sigmoid) scaling* fits a one-parameter logistic curve, $\hat{p} = 1 / (1 + \exp(A f + B))$, mapping the raw score $f$ to a probability via just two fitted numbers $A, B$. It is stable on small samples and ideal for the sigmoid-shaped distortion of under-confident models like random forests — but its rigid parametric shape cannot fix non-sigmoid errors.

*Isotonic regression* fits an arbitrary non-decreasing step function by least squares subject to monotonicity. It corrects *any* monotonic distortion and is more powerful, but it overfits on small datasets and needs a few thousand calibration points to behave. For multiclass neural networks, *temperature scaling* — dividing the logits by a single learned scalar $T$ before the softmax — is the standard lightweight fix; it sharpens or softens all probabilities at once without changing the predicted class, so accuracy is untouched.

The one thing you must not do is calibrate on the data the model trained on. An overfit classifier looks perfectly calibrated on its own training set, so the calibrator learns nothing and you ship overconfidence. Scikit-learn's `CalibratedClassifierCV` handles this with cross-validation: it fits the calibrator on out-of-fold predictions, keeping calibration data disjoint from training data.

::: {.callout-note title="Algorithm: calibrate and evaluate"}
1. Split off calibration data the base model never saw (or use cross-validated out-of-fold scores).
2. Fit the base classifier; obtain its raw scores on the held-out set.
3. Fit a calibrator — sigmoid, isotonic, or temperature — mapping raw scores to probabilities.
4. Evaluate on a *test* set with a reliability diagram plus Brier score, before and after.
:::

Here is the whole loop on a random forest, which tends to be under-confident:

::::{.panel-tabset}

### Python

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV, calibration_curve
from sklearn.metrics import brier_score_loss
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

np.random.seed(1988)

# Simulate a binary classification problem
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=20000, n_features=20, n_informative=6,
                           n_redundant=2, random_state=1988)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.5, random_state=1988)

# Random forests are typically under-confident (probabilities shrink toward 0.5)
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=1988).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
p_raw = rf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]

# Recalibrate on out-of-fold predictions: sigmoid (Platt) and isotonic
p_sig = CalibratedClassifierCV(rf, method="sigmoid",  cv=5).fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
p_iso = CalibratedClassifierCV(rf, method="isotonic", cv=5).fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]

# Brier score: lower is better (0 = perfect)
for name, p in [("raw RF", p_raw), ("sigmoid", p_sig), ("isotonic", p_iso)]:
    print(f"{name:9s} Brier = {brier_score_loss(y_te, p):.4f}")

# Reliability-diagram coordinates (observed frequency vs. mean predicted prob)
frac_pos, mean_pred = calibration_curve(y_te, p_raw, n_bins=10)
```

### R

```r
library(randomForest)

set.seed(1988)
n <- 20000; p <- 6
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
eta  <- X %*% c(1.5, -1, 0.8, -0.6, 0.5, -0.4)   # latent linear index
y    <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(eta))                # true probabilities -> labels
idx  <- sample(seq_len(n), n / 2)
train <- data.frame(y = factor(y[idx]),  X[idx, ])
test  <- data.frame(y = factor(y[-idx]), X[-idx, ])

# Random forest scores (typically under-confident)
rf         <- randomForest(y ~ ., data = train, ntree = 300)
score_te   <- predict(rf, test, type = "prob")[, 2]
score_oob  <- predict(rf, type = "prob")[, 2]      # out-of-bag scores on training data
ytr        <- as.integer(as.character(train$y))

# Platt (sigmoid) scaling: logistic fit of labels on the score
platt <- glm(ytr ~ score_oob, family = binomial)
p_sig <- predict(platt, data.frame(score_oob = score_te), type = "response")

# Isotonic regression: monotone step-function fit
iso   <- as.stepfun(isoreg(score_oob, ytr))
p_iso <- iso(score_te)

# Brier score: lower is better
yte   <- as.integer(as.character(test$y))
brier <- function(p, y) mean((p - y)^2)
c(raw = brier(score_te, yte), sigmoid = brier(p_sig, yte), isotonic = brier(p_iso, yte))
```
::::

## Bottom Line

- Calibration asks whether a predicted probability means what it says; a model can rank perfectly and still be badly miscalibrated.
- If you only need ranking or the argmax class, skip calibration — it changes nothing and can add noise.
- Calibrate when magnitudes drive decisions: expected value, fixed thresholds, probability arithmetic, or numbers shown to humans.
- Diagnose with a reliability diagram, not a Brier score alone — a proper scoring rule mixes calibration with discrimination.
- Fit the calibrator on held-out data: sigmoid for small samples and sigmoid-shaped error, isotonic when you have thousands of points, temperature scaling for neural nets.

## Where to Learn More

Platt (1999) introduced sigmoid scaling for SVM outputs, and Zadrozny and Elkan (2002) brought isotonic regression to calibration; both are short and foundational. Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005) is the classic empirical comparison across classifiers and the source of the "which models misbehave and how" intuition. Guo et al. (2017) revived the topic for deep learning and popularized temperature scaling. For a hands-on tour, the [scikit-learn calibration guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html) is excellent. Calibration also pairs naturally with [conformal prediction](https://vyasenov.github.io/blog/conformal-inference.html), a complementary route to trustworthy uncertainty.
